items.title: Video shows US Tomahawk missile hitting near Iran school that killed 175

featured_image.name: U.S. Tomahawk Hit Naval Base Beside Iranian School, Video Shows - The New  York Times

items.description:
Newly released video footage, authenticated by the investigative outlet Bellingcat, shows a US Tomahawk cruise missile striking an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval facility in Minab, Iran, on February 28 — the same location where a girls' elementary school was destroyed, killing at least 175 people, most of them children between the ages of 7 and 12.

The footage, originally released by Iran's Mehr News Agency and geolocated by Bellingcat, also captures smoke already rising from the vicinity of the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' school at the time the missile hits the adjacent IRGC compound. Bellingcat noted that the United States is the only participant in the conflict known to possess Tomahawk missiles, and that Israel does not operate the weapon. The findings add to a growing body of evidence from The New York Times, CNN, CBC, and NPR suggesting the US military was responsible for the deadliest single strike on civilians since the war began on February 28.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Yardeni raises market meltdown odds to 35% as Iran war widens

featured_image.name: US Stocks Face 35% Meltdown Probability This Year, Yardeni Warns - Bloomberg

items.description:
Veteran Wall Street strategist Ed Yardeni has sharply raised the probability of a market meltdown to 35% for the remainder of 2026, up from 20%, as the escalating war in Iran threatens to upend global energy markets and drag the U.S. economy toward stagflation. In what he described as "fast-moving times," the president of Yardeni Research also slashed his odds of a market meltup, according to Bloomberg.[1]

The revision marks a dramatic shift for one of Wall Street's most closely watched strategists, who just days earlier had maintained his meltdown estimate at 20% while predicting a "short war" scenario that would see oil prices fall quickly once hostilities ended.[2][3]

items.title: Energy Secretary Wright says Hormuz tanker traffic could resume within weeks

featured_image.name: Energy Secretary Says Tankers Could Start Moving Soon - The New York Times

items.description:
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that an oil tanker had successfully passed through the Strait of Hormuz, offering the first glimmer of hope that the critical waterway could resume regular shipping after being effectively shut down for nearly a week following U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran.

"We're not too long away, I think, before you'll see more regular resumption of ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz," Wright said on CNN's "State of the Union," adding that in a "worst case" scenario, full resumption could take "a few weeks, that's not months."[1][2]

items.title: Iran names Mojtaba Khamenei as new supreme leader

featured_image.name: Iran War: Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's Son, Mojtaba, Chosen as Next Supreme  Leader - Bloomberg

items.description: Iran's Assembly of Experts has selected Mojtaba Khamenei, the 56-year-old son of the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, as the country's new Supreme Leader, according to Reuters and Iranian state media reports on Sunday. The appointment marks the first hereditary transfer of power in the Islamic Republic's history — a system founded in 1979 on the explicit rejection of monarchy.[1][2]
